title: Punjab + Haryana, India
question: India reported that farm fires fell 93% between 2021 and 2025. Is that the whole story?
do: Monitor after 4 pm, add a geostationary feed to fire alerts, and report the early-afternoon count alongside the timing shift.
lesson: A drop in satellite counts can partly be burning moving to hours the satellites don’t see.

title: Punjab + Haryana, India
question: Does the same place show the same timing problem in its other burning season?
do: Use the record as it is for this season, with the range shown.
lesson: The check doesn’t say “timing matters” everywhere: this is the built-in control.

title: Kalimantan, Indonesia
question: 2019 was an extreme fire year. How far have fires fallen since, and can MODIS answer that?
do: Use the combined record, not a Terra or Aqua series, to report the decline.
lesson: The error can run the opposite way from Punjab: MODIS can exaggerate a decline.

title: Cerrado / MATOPIBA, Brazil
question: Did savanna clearing fires fall between 2019 and 2025?
do: After 2020, use the combined record rather than MODIS, and look at the whole series, not two years.
lesson: Satellite drift can bend a MODIS record even when burning hours haven’t changed.

title: California, USA
question: Were California’s 2025 wildfires worse than 2019’s?
do: Compare the whole series, not two years: wildfire years swing too much for a two-year headline.
lesson: Sometimes satellite timing isn’t the issue at all, and Burn Clock says so.

title: Paraná Delta, Argentina
question: Did burning in the delta wetlands change between 2019 and 2025?
do: Treat any two-year change here as unverified; there are too few fires for a timing verdict.
lesson: When the data can’t support a verdict, Burn Clock says “can’t tell”.
